cases.reason: 513 fields yield exactly 512 columns, and the truncation is silent — there is no flag and no error. Caught by 0 of the other cases: every one of them is far under the cap, so a binding that omitted the cap entirely would pass all of them.
JSON null is "null", not "object" — the first of typeof's two corrections. One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
an array is "array", not "object" — the second correction. One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
a JSON object is "object". One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
a JSON string is "string". One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
a JSON number is "number". One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
a JSON boolean is "boolean". One of the six §2.1 kinds reachable from JSON; a binding must produce exactly these six and no others.
A single trailing carriage return is removed before splitting, so a CRLF file's header does not end in a column named with a stray \r.
A line that is empty after trimming yields no columns at all, rather than one column with an empty name.

The second trim is not redundant: quotes are stripped before the inner whitespace, so '" a "' yields 'a'. Caught by 0 of the other cases — every other quoted field has no space inside its quotes, and a binding that trimmed only once would pass all of them.
Quote stripping requires the field to both begin and end with a double quote. A field with only a leading quote keeps it.

The split is on every comma with no quote awareness, so a quoted comma splits one field into two. Specified behaviour, not a defect: a binding implementing RFC 4180 quoting would return different columns from the same file. Caught by 0 of the other cases — no other case contains a comma inside quotes.

A UTF-8 BOM decodes to U+FEFF, which preamble §R7's set includes, so a BOM-prefixed header's first column is named without it. This is the case that fails a binding delegating to str.strip() or strings.TrimSpace, neither of which strips U+FEFF — and a BOM'd CSV is what Excel exports. Caught by 0 of the other cases.

Columns follow the object's key order, not sorted order. Caught by 0 of the other cases: this is the only one whose keys are not already alphabetical, so a Go binding decoding into a map and sorting would pass every other case.
A value's kind is reported without the value: a nested object and a nested array yield "object" and "array", and nothing about their contents is returned.
A line that parses to an array is not an object, so it yields no columns (§R6).
Unparseable input yields an absence, never an error (§R6).
An array whose first element is an object takes its columns from that element and its row count from the array's length.

The asymmetry: an empty array yields no columns but still carries a row count of 0. A binding short-circuiting to (no columns, no count) whenever it produces no columns fails here and passes everywhere else — caught by 0 of the other cases.
An array whose first element is not an object yields no columns, and still carries the array's length as the row count.
A top-level object yields its own columns and no row count — one record is not a count of records.
Anything that is neither an array nor an object yields neither columns nor a count.
Only elements carrying a type become columns; the root and group elements, which carry none, are skipped. That is what makes the result the leaf columns.
An absent schema yields no columns rather than an error (§R6).
An element whose name is not a string is skipped even when it carries a type — all three conditions must hold.

2^53+1 is returned as the nearest double, 2^53. Observable equality, not integer fidelity: a Python binding returning an exact int, or a Go binding returning an int64, would preserve MORE information and fail this case — which is §6.1's point. Caught by 0 of the other cases: every other row count is small enough to be exact.
A num_rows that is neither a number nor a wide integer yields an absence rather than a coerced zero.
With no newline the whole text is the first line, and the count is one.
A trailing newline does not add a line: two newlines with a trailing one is two lines, not three.
Without a trailing newline the final partial line still counts.
A truncated read yields no count at all — a count over a partial read would be a wrong number rather than an estimate.
A trailing carriage return is NOT removed here — §3 removes it, and only for CSV. Caught by 0 of the other §7 cases, none of which contains a carriage return.

An empty input has zero lines. The reference implementation returned 1 until this case was added: the count is nl + 1 whenever the text does not end with a newline, and the Math.max(0, ...) floor could never catch a sum that is never negative. This case is what found it, and the correction is registered in RFC-0017 section 6.1. Caught by 0 of the other cases: every other text is non-empty.

truncated is checked before the empty-input rule, so an empty truncated read is an absence rather than zero. Without this case a binding could implement §7.1 by special-casing the empty string ahead of the truncation check and still pass.
